items.title: Drought Intensifies Across Puerto Rico
items.short_description: Rainfall deficits and high temperatures have created unusually dry conditions and have spurred water shortages on much of the tropical archipelago.
items.abstract: Rainfall deficits and high temperatures have created unusually dry conditions and have spurred water shortages on much of the tropical archipelago. The dry conditions have contributed to water shortages and rationing in some areas, leading Puerto Rico’s governor to declare a state of emergency in late July and the U.S. government to issue a drought disaster declaration for more than two dozen cities and towns in late August. For recent updates to Puerto Rico’s drought maps, satellite estimates of soil moisture, as well as weather, streamflow, and well observations, were particularly important factors, he said. As of August 25, 2026, three-quarters of Puerto Rico was experiencing at least moderate drought, according to the group’s assessment. Strained water resources have affected farmers, ranchers, and residents across the territory.

items.title: Ice Island Survives Run-In With Joe Island
items.short_description: In summer 2026, a substantial iceberg calved from Petermann Glacier in northwest Greenland and swiftly drifted into Nares Strait, colliding with an island along the way.
items.abstract: In summer 2026, a substantial iceberg calved from Petermann Glacier in northwest Greenland and swiftly drifted into Nares Strait, colliding with an island along the way. The team reported that the large tabular iceberg, or “ice island,” measured just over 76 square kilometers (29 square miles) at the time it calved—the largest to break from the glacier since the ice island of 2012 (130 square kilometers). Glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College has also been tracking the iceberg, using images from NASA-USGS Landsat satellites, as it drifted down Petermann Fjord toward Nares Strait. Wind and surface currents have swept it out of the fjord, and satellite images show it pivoting away from Joe Island and continuing southwest through Nares Strait.

items.title: Pasterze Hangs on as Austria’s Largest Glacier
items.short_description: One narrowing icefall remains the linchpin for the Alpine glacier—and it may not be long for this world.
items.abstract: One narrowing icefall remains the linchpin for the Alpine glacier—and it may not be long for this world. The last icefall connecting the upper and lower portions of the Pasterze Glacier in the Eastern Alps appeared poised to break, which would put an end to its reign as the country’s largest. In retreat since the mid-1800s, the Pasterze has lost mass almost continuously and at increasing rates since 1980, according to scientists from the University of Graz, GeoSphere Austria, and the Austrian Alpine Club. Between 1998 and 2025, scientists from the University of Graz monitored the width of the icefall, finding a decrease from nearly 900 meters (3,000 feet) to just 120 meters (390 feet). When Pasterze’s Hufeisenbruch icefall does succumb to melting or collapse, the glacier will cede its status as Austria’s largest to Gepatschferner in the Ötztal Alps in Tyrol.

items.title: The Forested Floodplains of Congaree National Park
items.short_description: The meandering Congaree River sustains towering forest ecosystems and fashions oxbow lakes as it shifts across its floodplain.
items.abstract: The meandering Congaree River sustains towering forest ecosystems and fashions oxbow lakes as it shifts across its floodplain. Among the 63 U.S. national parks, few are as defined by a single river's floodplain as Congaree National Park in South Carolina. While the features are also prominent in other parks, a full 80 percent of Congaree National Park lies within the Congaree River floodplain. On the right side of the image is Bates Old River, a roughly 4-mile-long abandoned channel of the Congaree River and one of the longest oxbow lakes in South Carolina. While loggers targeted forests along the Congaree in the 1880s, challenges such as frequent flooding, interminably muddy roads, and mosquito-plagued conditions meant that most of the floodplain forests escaped the widespread logging that transformed other parts of the Southeast.

items.title: Rare, Widespread Snow in the Atacama Desert
items.short_description: Back-to-back winter storms in August 2026 brought snowfall to northern Chile, from the Andes to near the Pacific coast.
items.abstract: Back-to-back winter storms in August 2026 brought snowfall to northern Chile, from the Andes to near the Pacific coast. In August 2026, back-to-back winter storms left parts of the Atacama Desert in northern Chile covered in a rare blanket of snow. This image, captured by the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA's Terra satellite on August 19, shows snow extending westward from the Andes, across the desert’s hyper-arid core, and close to the Pacific coast south of the Chilean port city of Antofagasta. The atmospheric disruption, combined with ample coastal moisture, produced precipitation that spanned an unusually wide swath of the region—offshore, along the coast, across the core of the Atacama, and over the Andes. In addition to the August storms, a major event in July brought significant impacts to the country’s Norte Chico region.

items.title: A Changing World for Emperor Penguins
items.short_description: Experts are analyzing decades of images from Landsat satellites for clues about how the iconic birds have responded to sea ice disruptions in the past.
items.abstract: Experts are analyzing decades of images from Landsat satellites for clues about how the iconic birds have responded to sea ice disruptions in the past. Meanwhile, some models project that emperor penguins could disappear by 2100 due to their habitats becoming inhospitable. However, new research, based on decades of observations from NASA-USGS Landsat satellites, offers some hope, underscoring that many colonies have persisted for decades and that emperor penguins may be more flexible about where they breed than previously thought. Except for a few well-studied colonies, scientists have known little about how long many emperor penguin colonies have existed, how their populations have changed, or how they have responded to past disruptions in landfast sea ice. The image above on the right shows the colony in December 2025, the most recent month Landsat has observed the colony.
